title: THE “SONS OF GOD” TOOK WOMEN THEY DESIRED: WHAT IS GENESIS 6 ACTUALLY DESCRIBING?
paragraphs: THE “SONS OF GOD” TOOK WOMEN THEY DESIRED: WHAT IS GENESIS 6 ACTUALLY DESCRIBING?

Angels? Powerful rulers? The sons of Seth? Giants? Demonic corruption? Before you decide what Genesis 6 means, look closely at what the Bible actually says—because the most frightening part of this passage may not be the Nephilim at all.
There is a sentence buried near the beginning of the Bible that has disturbed, fascinated, and divided readers for centuries.
It is only a few words long.
But once you notice it, it is difficult to forget.
“The sons of God saw the daughters of men that they were fair; and they took them wives of all which they chose.”
And only a few verses later, God looked upon the earth and saw something horrifying:
“The wickedness of man was great in the earth.”
Who were these mysterious “sons of God”?
Were they fallen heavenly beings who crossed a boundary established by God?
Were they powerful human rulers who treated women as possessions?
Were they descendants of Seth abandoning covenant faithfulness and joining themselves to the ungodly line?
And what about the mysterious Nephilim?
Were they the children produced by these unions?
Were they violent warriors whose reputation became legendary?
Genesis does not answer every question we want answered.
And that may be part of the point.

Because while people have spent centuries staring at the mystery of Genesis 6, it is possible to become so fascinated with the identity of the “sons of God” that we miss the horrifying diagnosis God gives of the human heart.
The chapter is not ultimately about satisfying our curiosity concerning strange beings.
It is about a world drowning in rebellion.
And somewhere inside this ancient story...
The Hebrew deserves to be heard.
“sons of God” or “sons of the God.”
Similar language appears in Job 1:6 and Job 2:1, where “sons of God” present themselves before the LORD, and Job 38:7 uses comparable language when describing heavenly beings rejoicing at creation.
That is one major reason an ancient interpretation understands Genesis 6 as describing heavenly beings who rebelled against God's appointed order.
This interpretation is not some modern internet conspiracy theory.

Ancient Jewish literature interpreted the passage this way, and many Christians throughout history have connected Genesis 6 with passages such as Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4, where angels who sinned are described as being kept for judgment.
“kept not their first estate, but left their own habitation.”
Jude does not explicitly say, “These are the beings mentioned in Genesis 6.”
Second Peter does not explicitly identify Genesis 6 either.
The connection is ancient and significant, but we should not turn an inference into a sentence Scripture itself never writes.
Jesus said that in the resurrection people “neither marry, nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven” (Matthew 22:30).
Some readers therefore reject the angelic interpretation entirely.
Others respond that Jesus specifically describes angels in heaven, whereas Genesis 6, on the angelic interpretation, concerns rebellious beings doing precisely what they were never authorized to do.
And Christians who love Scripture have stood on more than one side of it.
Another longstanding interpretation sees the “sons of God” as human beings—often understood as the godly line associated with Seth—who intermarried with women from an ungodly society.
Genesis has just traced two contrasting trajectories.
Cain's line becomes associated with escalating violence. Lamech boasts of killing a man and magnifies vengeance.
“Then began men to call upon the name of the LORD.”
Under the Sethite interpretation, Genesis 6 records the collapse of that separation.
Those associated with worship of God began choosing according to desire rather than covenant faithfulness.
There is also a third major interpretation.
Some understand the “sons of God” as kings, nobles, tyrants, or powerful rulers who claimed extraordinary status and accumulated women according to their desires.
Ancient rulers could portray themselves in exalted or divine terms, and the language of Genesis 6:2 sounds ominously like unrestricted power:
“they took them wives of all which they chose.”
Different interpretations disagree about the identity of the actors.
Under every major interpretation, the direction of the story is downward.
Then comes one of the strangest words in the Old Testament:
“There were giants in the earth in those days...”
Many English readers know the word through the translation “giants.”
But the Hebrew term itself does not simply mean “giants” with the precision modern readers sometimes assume.
Nephilim occurs only here and in Numbers 13:33.
The ancient Greek Septuagint rendered the term with γίγαντες — gigantes, which contributed to the longstanding “giants” tradition.
But Genesis itself does not stop to define their anatomy, calculate their height, or give us a biological explanation for them.
Instead, Genesis 6:4 moves toward language of reputation and power:
“mighty men which were of old, men of renown.”
“men of the name”—commonly rendered “men of renown.”
And there is an important detail sensational retellings sometimes skip.
Genesis 6:4 does not state as unambiguously as people often assume that the Nephilim were necessarily the offspring of the “sons of God” and “daughters of men.”
It says the Nephilim were on the earth “in those days—and also afterward,” and then mentions the sons of God going in to the daughters of men and children being born.
The relationship between those clauses has been debated for centuries.
So we should refuse to make Scripture say more than Scripture says.
Perhaps the “sons of God” were rebellious heavenly beings.
Perhaps the passage is describing catastrophic human covenant compromise.
Perhaps tyrannical rulers are in view.
Christians can examine the evidence carefully.
But Genesis does not permit us to miss what happens next.
Because verse 5 removes almost every mystery.
Not the mystery of the Nephilim.
The mystery of why judgment came.
“And GOD saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth.”
“And that every imagination of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually.”
There is the monster Genesis wants you to see.
And it is much closer than we would like.
We love mysteries because mysteries allow us to examine something outside ourselves.
Were the sons of God angels?
What happened in the unseen realm?
But there is another question Genesis forces upon us:
And that question becomes uncomfortable because the answer eventually reaches beyond Noah's generation.
Genesis 6 begins with seeing and taking.
Eve “saw” that the tree was good for food.
Again and again, sin whispers the same ancient lie:
If you desire it, you deserve it.
Nobody has the right to tell you no.
That is where Genesis 6 suddenly stops feeling ancient.
Because maybe you have never wondered whether angels could produce children with humans.
But you know what desire feels like.
You know what it is to want something God has forbidden.
You know how easily a heart can rename lust “love.”
That is what makes Genesis 6 terrifying.
And God saw a civilization rotting from the inside.
Jesus later used Noah's generation as a warning.
The terrifying thing about judgment is that ordinary life can continue right up until the moment ordinary life ends.
A sentence quieter than the violence.
More important than all the speculation.
“But Noah found grace in the eyes of the LORD.”
Before Noah stepped onto dry ground after the flood.
Noah found favor in the eyes of the LORD.
And Noah found grace in the eyes of God.
And that thread of grace keeps moving through Scripture until it reaches a wooden cross outside Jerusalem.
Noah's ark was not the final rescue.
Noah was not the final righteous man.
The flood did not permanently cure the human heart.
In fact, after the waters receded, Genesis would again acknowledge the persistent bent of the human heart toward evil.
Humanity needed something greater than surviving water.
Jesus Christ came into the same human story.
And unlike everyone before Him, Christ did not surrender to sin.
He remained faithful where humanity rebelled.
And there, the truly righteous Son gave Himself for the guilty.
The Gospel does not tell you that your sin is insignificant.
The cross tells you your sin was so serious that redemption cost the blood of Christ.
But the empty tomb tells you something else.
Your scandal does not have to write your final chapter.
That is why repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is the sinner finally stopping the exhausting attempt to hide from the One who already sees everything.
That addiction you keep deleting from your history.
That resentment you smile over every Sunday.
That relationship you know is pulling you away from Him.
The wound you turned into an excuse to wound other people.
Not because sin does not matter.
Because Christ is sufficient for sinners who come to Him.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Maybe the question that brought you into this article was:
Who were the sons of God?
But perhaps the question God is pressing into your heart now is:
What are you allowing yourself to desire?
What have you begun taking that God never gave you permission to take?
What boundary are you slowly convincing yourself no longer matters?
What sin have you studied long enough to explain but never surrendered long enough to forsake?
Biblical knowledge without repentance can become another hiding place.
You can know Hebrew words and still hide sin.
You can debate Nephilim and still neglect Jesus.
You can win an argument about Genesis 6 while losing the battle taking place inside your own heart.
Do not let fascination with the mysterious distract you from the unmistakable.
And sinners are called to repent and believe the Gospel.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to publish the details of your private sin. But you can make a simple confession of need.

And if Christ has already brought you out of something you thought would destroy you, tell somebody what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another exhausted believer desperately needed to read tonight.
Not because every interpretive question in Genesis 6 has been solved—Scripture does not give us permission to pretend that.
Come back when desire starts rewriting God's boundaries.
And not because Christians can purchase their way into obedience.

But generosity, sharing biblical truth, supporting faithful ministry, encouraging other believers, and using what God has entrusted to us for Gospel work can all become expressions of Christian stewardship when they are done freely, wisely, and for God's glory.
And there is more available even without purchasing anything.
If these resources strengthen you, share them.
Invite the person who has quietly walked away from church.
Invite the Christian who is spiritually starving but embarrassed to admit it.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who keeps asking questions you cannot always answer.
Most of all, pray that they encounter Christ.
We should be humble enough to admit that.
But its central warning is not mysterious.
And somehow, standing in the darkness of that generation, one breathtaking word survived.
That word would travel through an ark.
Until grace appeared not merely as an idea...
but in the person of Jesus Christ.
So perhaps the most important question after reading Genesis 6 is not whether you can identify every mysterious being in the chapter.
Perhaps it is whether you have run to the One who can rescue you from the darkness inside your own heart.
Because the greatest monster in Genesis 6 was never something enormous walking across the earth.
It was sin ruling the human heart.
And the greatest wonder in the Bible is not the Nephilim.
It is that a holy God still chose to rescue sinners.
Remember this when your past whispers that you are permanently disqualified:
The flood could wash a world clean on the outside, but only Jesus can make a sinner new from the inside.
